Section 321 can eliminate ordinary duty on qualifying shipments valued at $800 or less, and its appeal is that it avoids importing a large batch into the United States before selling it. [shard_03728_43299] [shard_04647_72515]

That saving is not the same as “no customs responsibility,” because shipments still need accurate descriptions, must meet safety requirements, and can be delayed when the information is inadequate. [shard_03728_43299] [shard_04649_36644]

The real comparison is landed cost, not factory price: add parcel postage, air-freight surcharges, customs-broker or platform fees, payment and refund leakage, lost packages, customer-service labor, returns, compliance work, and the cost of occasional holds or rule changes.

Direct shipping can make sense for lightweight, inexpensive, non-regulated products with strong gross margins, low return rates, and customers who accept slower delivery, but it is much less attractive when a missed delivery promise damages a small brand’s reputation.

Standard air freight from China to the United States is described as roughly 8–10 days in transit, while express service may reduce that by about two or three days, and the final customer delivery time also depends on the seller, shipping method, handoffs, and customs processing. Air freight is therefore not a fixed per-order bargain: capacity, fuel and peak-season pricing can change, and shipping many tiny parcels may cost more than consolidating inventory into a lower-cost international shipment and fulfilling domestically.

The compliance risk is material because a direct-to-consumer parcel does not make the product’s origin, materials, factory labor, safety status, or intellectual-property position disappear.

Concerns about forced-labor disclosures and China-dependent supplier networks have already been raised in connection with major ecommerce businesses, so a small seller should demand factory identities, production addresses, bills of materials, labor attestations, and an auditable chain of custody rather than accept a supplier’s generic “compliant” certificate. Holding fast-moving inventory in a US warehouse usually sacrifices some of the Section 321 cash-flow advantage but gives you consolidated import economics, more predictable delivery, easier inspection and returns, and a service level that is easier to protect; the trade-off is inventory risk and working capital.
